lessonTitle: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and nonce reuse
question: Why is the user id passed as associated data instead of being encrypted with the message?
options: The server needs to read it to route the message, but it must still be bound to the ciphertext so it cannot be swapped
Associated data is encrypted twice
Associated data makes the ciphertext shorter
It lets the server skip tag verification
explain: Associated data stays readable but is covered by the tag. Changing it (for example to another user's id) makes decryption fail, as the code shows.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
question: You have a 32-byte random shared secret from a key exchange and need an encryption key and a MAC key. Which tool fits?
options: HKDF with two different info labels
Argon2id with high memory
SHA-1 of the secret, split in half
Use the secret directly for both
explain: The input is already high-entropy, so no stretching is needed. HKDF extracts and expands it into independent keys per label.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Elliptic curves and digital signatures: the PS3 and CurveBall
question: What was the root cause of CurveBall?
options: Certificate validation matched the public key without checking the curve parameters it belonged to
SHA-1 collisions in certificates
A weak random number generator in Windows
ECDSA nonce reuse by Microsoft
explain: A public key only means something together with its curve and generator. Accepting attacker-chosen parameters let the attacker choose a generator for which they knew the private key.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: You compose a data tensor A with B and get R = A o B. Which property does the CuTe documentation guarantee?
options: R has the same shape as A
R is always injective
R(i) = A(B(i)) for all i in B's domain, and R accepts B's coordinates
R has the same strides as B
explain: Composition's post-conditions are compatible(B, R) and R(i) == A(B(i)). B defines the domain, so R takes B's coordinates; A defines where those land.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: Why can't a CPU vendor simply add many more DDR5 channels to every socket?
options: DDR5 does not support more than two channels per socket
More channels would make memory non-coherent
Each DDR5 channel is a wide parallel interface that needs many pins (Sun et al. cite 288 per channel), and the package pin budget is fixed
Linux cannot address more than eight memory channels
explain: DDR is a wide parallel interface. Capacity and bandwidth scale with the number of channels, and each channel eats a lot of pins. A serial CXL link delivers more bandwidth per pin, which is why it is attractive for expansion.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: TPP does not promote a slow-tier page on its first NUMA hinting fault if the page is on the inactive LRU list. What problem does this avoid?
options: Deadlock between the fault handler and reclaim
Ping-pong: an infrequently used page is promoted, then quickly demoted again, wasting migration bandwidth
Running out of tier-16 memory
Breaking cache coherence on the CXL link
explain: A single touch does not prove a page is hot. Promoting it would push something else out of DRAM, and under pressure the promoted page would soon be demoted again. Requiring the page to be on the active LRU adds hysteresis: a page must show repeated use before it moves, so it stops flipping back and forth.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
question: Which statement about Base64 is correct?
options: It is a weak form of encryption that needs a short key
It is an encoding that anyone can reverse without a key, so it protects nothing
It is a hash, so the original cannot be recovered
It is only used for images
explain: Base64 (RFC 4648) maps bytes to 64 printable characters so they survive text channels. Decoding needs no secret. When officials said the reporter had 'unencrypted the source code' or 'decoded the HTML source code', they made an ordinary step sound like an attack.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
question: Which change did the 2021 rulemaking make to the security research exemption, according to GitHub's summary?
options: It made circumvention tools legal to sell
It removed the condition that the research must not violate any other law
It ended the exemption
It extended the exemption to servers you do not own without permission
explain: GitHub explains that before 2021 a violation of another law such as the CFAA could also cost you the DMCA exemption. The Office recommended removing that condition, while noting researchers must still consider other laws themselves.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
question: Under the ISC2 complaint procedure, who may complain that a member breached Canon III (diligent and competent service to principals)?
options: Any member of the public
Only principals, meaning those with an employer or contractor relationship with the member
Only other certified professionals
Nobody: Canon III is advisory
explain: ISC2's procedure says anyone may complain about Canons I or II, only principals about Canon III, and only other professionals who subscribe to a code of ethics about Canon IV.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
question: Why is tuning the mixture directly on downstream benchmarks risky, beyond its cost?
options: Benchmarks are measured in accuracy, not loss
Downstream tuning always picks uniform weights
The mixture can overfit to the specific benchmarks used, which may not reflect the many tasks the model will face
explain: A pretrained model is used for many tasks nobody listed in advance. A mixture tuned to a handful of benchmarks can trade away performance elsewhere. DoReMi deliberately uses no downstream data.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Knobs, failure modes, and what came after DoReMi
question: You start DoReMi from uniform reference weights on a corpus where one domain is tiny. After one round, results are no better than baseline. What is the paper's recommended next move?
options: Run iterated DoReMi: train a new reference model on the round-1 weights and run again
Increase the proxy to 1B parameters
Set the smoothing c to 0 so weak domains disappear
Copy the published Pile weights
explain: On GLaM, round 1 from uniform weights was only comparable to the baseline, and round 2 matched downstream-tuned weights. A suboptimal reference gives a suboptimal excess loss; iterating fixes the reference. Bigger proxies did worse in the paper.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: Why do pipelines run heuristic rules before a perplexity filter or a model-based classifier?
options: Rules are more accurate than models
The order does not matter for cost
Rules only count words and symbols, so they cheaply remove obvious junk before the expensive model-based steps run
Perplexity filters only work on text that has been deduplicated
explain: A rule is a few counts per page; a language model or classifier must process every token. Removing describable junk first shrinks what the costly steps must score. Orders still vary between pipelines.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
question: In `soa<8> Point pts[...]` (float x, y, z), what is the byte offset of `pts[17].z` from the start of the array?
explain: Block 2 (17 divided by 8 is 2, rounded down), lane 1 (the remainder). Each block is 96 bytes and z is the third 32-byte run. Offset = 2 x 96 + 2 x 32 + 1 x 4 = 260. 212 is the AoS answer (17 x 12 + 8), 204 is where record 17 starts in AoS, and 68 is plain SoA (17 x 4).

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
question: A Purview-style rule finds a Luhn-valid 16-digit number with no keywords or dates within 300 characters. What should the confidence be?
options: Low: pattern and checksum without supporting context
High: the checksum proves it is a card
None: without a keyword it is discarded
High, because test numbers are excluded
explain: In Microsoft's documented definition, pattern plus checksum alone is the low-confidence pattern (65). High confidence (85) needs one of the context conditions. About 1 in 10 random numbers pass Luhn, so the checksum alone proves little.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves
question: A team wants to encrypt an `is_vip` boolean column but still filter on it. Why is deterministic encryption a poor choice?
options: Deterministic encryption cannot encrypt booleans
It is slower than randomized encryption
It requires a secure enclave
With only two values, each ciphertext appears in many rows, and counting them (plus any known fact about one row) reveals every row's value
explain: Deterministic encryption maps each plaintext to one ciphertext. With two possible values, there are two ciphertexts; knowing the VIP rate or one VIP customer decodes all rows. Microsoft's documentation warns about exactly this for True/False columns.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
question: A DLP rule has 95% recall and a 1% false positive rate. Real leaks are 1 in 1,000 messages. Roughly what share of its alerts are real?
options: About 9%
About 95%
About 50%
About 1%
explain: Per 200,000 messages: 190 true alerts and about 1,998 false ones, so 190 / 2,188 is about 8.7%. Recall is 95%, but precision is low because clean messages vastly outnumber leaks.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
question: Branch servers had disk encryption switched on years after deployment, and the product encrypted only newly written data. Why does a later cryptographic erase not sanitise them?
options: The data written before encryption was enabled is still plaintext on the disks, and destroying the key does nothing to it
Crypto erase never works on servers
The keys were too short
Crypto erase needs internet access
explain: Cryptographic erase only removes access to what was encrypted. SP 800-88 Rev. 2 makes 'no sensitive data previously stored in plaintext' a precondition, and the SEC order describes exactly this flaw.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
question: Two requests arrive with the same seed and the same temperature, and the sampler draws from one shared RNG stream. What does request B's token depend on?
options: How many draws the sampler already consumed for other requests, so B's token depends on the traffic around it.
Nothing beyond its own seed, since the seed fully determines the stream.
Only the temperature, because the seed is consumed once at startup.
The order in which atomic adds landed in the final GEMM.
explain: A shared stream makes the position in the stream part of the request's input, and that position is set by the queue. Seeding the stream fixes the sequence of numbers, not which element of it your request receives. Per-request generator state is what removes the dependency.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
question: Why does the toy simulator put a sequence number between the time and the event in each queue entry?
options: So events at the same simulated time pop in a fixed order on every run
To make the heap faster
To count how many messages were lost
So that later events can be cancelled
explain: Two events can share a timestamp. Without a deterministic tie-breaker their order would depend on incidental details (here, Python would even try to compare the event payloads). The sequence number makes the order a function of the order of scheduling, which is itself determined by the seed.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud
question: Which item is policy as code?
options: A Terraform file that creates an S3 bucket
A GitHub Actions workflow that runs unit tests
A Rego file stating that no security group may allow SSH from 0.0.0.0/0
A wiki page listing the company's security standards
explain: Policy as code is a rule a machine evaluates. The Terraform file is infrastructure as code, the workflow is pipeline code, and a wiki page is policy that nobody's pipeline can enforce.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
question: After a CI vendor breach, which kind of pipeline credential needs no rotation at all?
options: A long-lived cloud access key stored as a project secret
An SSH deploy key stored in the CI service
A registry token kept in a context
A cloud role assumed through OIDC, where the CI service stores only the role name
explain: With OIDC the CI service holds no long-lived secret: it presents a short-lived signed token each run. Stolen role names grant nothing. Every stored key or token must be rotated.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Terraform state: the file that holds every secret
question: Grzelak's attack adds a resource that names an attacker's provider to the state. Why does a required manual approval before apply not stop it?
options: Approvals are optional in Terraform
terraform init downloads the provider and Terraform runs its code while planning, before anyone is asked to approve
The provider runs only after apply
State files are not read during plan
explain: Grzelak notes that even if the reviewer rejects the plan, the code has already executed. That is why the post recommends pre-installed providers in an immutable image and a read-only role for the plan step.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code
question: During an outage an engineer raised a database's connection limit in the console, and the fix should stay. What is the right drift response?
options: Run apply to revert it, since code is the source of truth
Codify it: change the Terraform code through a pull request to match, using refresh-only planning to reconcile state, so the next apply does not undo it
Delete the database from state
Ignore the drift alerts from now on
explain: This is the codify path. Reverting would reintroduce the outage; ignoring trains everyone to ignore drift alerts.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
question: Spot the bug: a colleague's loss is `(ce * masked).sum() / masked.sum()`, the plain average over masked tokens, with t still drawn uniformly. What changes?
options: Nothing; it is the same quantity
The loss now includes visible tokens

Summed over the batch and divided by the total masked count, every masked token gets equal weight, so heavily masked sequences dominate; the 1/t factor is lost and it is no longer the likelihood bound
The model will learn to predict [MASK] tokens
explain: Over a large batch the ratio tends to E[sum of masked losses] / E[count]: the unweighted MaskGIT-style objective with no 1/t, which LLaDA notes lacks a link to maximum likelihood. The principled loss divides each sequence by t L. Dividing each sequence by its own masked count would actually be fine: with uniform t the count is uniform on 0 to L, giving the exact-count form LLaDA uses for likelihoods.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
question: System A serves 9 req/s on 3 GPUs at 92% attainment. System B serves 4 req/s on 1 GPU at 91% attainment, and 4.5 req/s at 85%. Assuming these are the largest rates meeting 90%, which has higher per-GPU goodput?
options: They tie, since both exceed 90%
A, because 9 req/s is more than 4 req/s
B, with 4 req/s per GPU against A's 3
B, with 4.5 req/s per GPU
explain: Per-GPU goodput divides the highest rate meeting the attainment goal by the GPU count: A gives 9/3 = 3 req/s per GPU and B gives 4/1 = 4. B's 4.5 req/s point misses the 90% goal, so it does not count.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What storage remembers: the BTK floppy disk (2005)
question: An examiner has recovered the deleted files and now asks: does data showing use by "Dennis" on a church computer identify the sender, and how strongly? Which NIST SP 800-86 phase is this?
options: Analysis
Collection
Examination
Reporting
explain: Recovering the files and their metadata was examination. Weighing what the facts mean for the question being asked is analysis. Reporting comes after, when the conclusion and its limits are written down.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Eight NTFS timestamps, and how timestomping gets caught
question: Why is last-access time weak evidence on NTFS?
options: It is stored only in FN, which users cannot see
Updates to it can be deferred by up to an hour and can be disabled entirely
It uses local time instead of UTC
It records the time the antivirus scanned the file
explain: Microsoft documents that NTFS may defer last-access updates by up to one hour and that the update can be turned off (disablelastaccess). It is a FILETIME in UTC and exists in SI too.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Carving: recovering files with no metadata at all
question: Why does carving deleted files from a Windows 11 laptop's NVMe SSD usually fail?
options: NVMe drives do not use sectors
With delete notifications (TRIM) on by default, the drive is told freed blocks are unused and typically clears them
Windows 11 encrypts deleted files with a separate key
Carving only works on FAT
explain: Delete notification tells the drive which clusters were freed, and the drive's garbage collection makes them read back empty. CyBOK cites near-zero recovery on TRIM-aware systems. Carving is file system independent, and NVMe still exposes blocks.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Mobile forensics: extraction levels, encryption and isolation
question: Why does NIST caution that logical extraction may modify data?
options: The connection type and protocol used to talk to the phone can change data on it, for example marking unread SMS as read
Logical extraction always wipes the phone
Logical extraction writes a forensic agent into the bootloader
It uses JTAG, which resets memory
explain: SP 800-101r1 notes that different connection methods and protocols may modify data, giving unread SMS as the example. It does not wipe the phone, and JTAG is level 3, not logical.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence law and writing the expert report
question: Your analysis shows a USB stick with VSN 1234-ABCD was mounted and a document on it was opened from the profile of user jsmith. Which sentence belongs in the opinion section?
options: J. Smith stole the payroll file
The jsmith profile opened payroll_export.csv from a removable volume with serial 1234-ABCD; this is consistent with, but does not by itself establish, J. Smith personally doing so
The USB stick belongs to J. Smith
No conclusions can be drawn from artefacts
explain: The opinion should state what the artefacts support (an account and a volume) and its limits. Attributing the act to a person or ownership of the stick needs other evidence; saying nothing ignores real findings.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA: a fixed-degree graph built for GPUs
question: A CAGRA graph built with intermediate degree 128 and graph degree 64 gives too low recall even with large search settings. Per the cuVS tuning guide, what is the build-side knob to try after graph_degree?
options: Lower intermediate_graph_degree
Disable reverse edges
Increase intermediate_graph_degree, giving pruning more choices
Set alpha = 1.2
explain: cuVS suggests tuning itopk_size (the search-time list size, covered in the next lesson) first, then graph_degree, then intermediate_graph_degree if graph quality is still too low. A larger kNN graph gives the pruning step more candidates, at a higher build cost. CAGRA has no alpha parameter.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
question: Why does DPO's regularization fail on a pair that appears once in the data?
options: Because DPO forgets to load the reference model
Because the empirical preference for that pair is 1, and fitting probability 1 with a sigmoid needs an unbounded log-ratio gap regardless of beta
Because beta is too large by default
Because the gradient weight grows as the margin grows
explain: One label means the observed preference is 1. The logistic loss can always be lowered further by widening the gap, so the optimum sits at infinity and beta only changes the speed. The weight actually shrinks with the margin; that slows drift but never stops it.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
question: A dual write does `old.increment(counter, 1)` then `new.increment(counter, 1)`, retrying the second call on timeout. After a week the new counters are slightly *higher* than the old ones. What is the most likely cause?
options: Clock skew between the two stores
A timed-out increment had actually been applied, so the retry applied it twice
The backfill copied counters that were already migrated
Last-writer-wins dropped some increments in the old store
explain: A timeout does not mean the write failed. Retrying a non-idempotent delta (add 1) after an ambiguous failure double-applies it. Writing the full current value read from the source of truth, or making the operation idempotent with a request ID, removes the problem.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
question: Why is a kernel module a poor way to add ad hoc tracing to a production machine, compared with an eBPF program?
options: A module cannot read kernel function arguments
Nothing checks the module's code before it runs, so one bad pointer or endless loop can crash or hang the whole machine
Modules can only be loaded at boot time
Modules run in user space and are therefore slow
explain: Modules run arbitrary native code in the kernel with no load-time safety proof. eBPF programs are verified first (termination, initialized registers, in-bounds memory) and only then JIT-compiled and attached.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: Many CPUs increment the same counter. Why does bpftrace recommend @c = count() over @c++?
options: count() uses per-CPU slots, so concurrent updates never collide; @c++ is a non-atomic shared update that can lose increments
@c++ is rejected by the verifier
count() is faster to read than @c++
@c++ sends an event to user space each time
explain: Per-CPU maps make writes cheap and exact. The trade is that reading the value is slower, since every CPU's slot must be summed.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Integer-only inference: int8 multiplies, int32 accumulators
question: A team accumulates int8 x int8 products in an int16 register to save space. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, products of 8-bit numbers always fit in 16 bits
Sums overflow: one product can reach about 32,000, so two products can already exceed the int16 maximum
The zero point can no longer be represented
The scale M stops being in (0, 1)
explain: A single product fits in 16 bits, but the dot product adds hundreds or thousands of them. Jacob et al. use an int32 accumulator for exactly this reason. ONNX Runtime documents a related issue with VPMADDUBSW, an x86 vector instruction (AVX2, AVX-512) that adds pairs of 8-bit products into 16 bits and clamps on overflow.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
question: FortiOS/FortiProxy has 15 KEV entries (12 ransomware-linked); F5 BIG-IP has 8. What can you conclude from these counts alone?
options: BIG-IP is about twice as secure as FortiOS
FortiOS should be banned
Little about code quality: KEV records exploitation that was found and reported, which also depends on how common and attractive a product is
KEV only covers network products
explain: KEV is evidence of exploitation in the wild, not a defect rate. Deployment size, attacker interest and who investigates all affect the count. Use it to decide what to watch and patch fastest, not to grade vendors on its own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
question: On 10 January 2024 Ivanti published a mitigation, with patches still weeks away. Which of these did applying the mitigation NOT do?
options: Remove webshells, modified files and stolen passwords from devices already compromised
Block the known route to the vulnerable endpoints
Reduce exposure while waiting for patches
Buy time for a planned rebuild
explain: A mitigation stops new exploitation by the known path. It does nothing about what the attacker already changed or took, which is why Volexity said a mitigation does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
question: Does BOD 23-02 require an agency to take its public VPN portal off the internet?
options: Yes, all VPN services must be internal
No. It covers management interfaces; the VPN service itself may stay public (other rules, such as patch deadlines, still apply to it)
Yes, unless the portal sits behind a separate policy enforcement point
No, because VPN portals count as cloud management interfaces, which are out of scope
explain: The directive defines a networked management interface as one meant exclusively for administrators. The user-facing VPN service is the device's job, so it is not in scope, although BOD 26-04 still sets its patch deadlines.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
question: Why do Chen et al. measure outcome efficiency instead of just counting tokens?
options: Token counts cannot be compared across tokenizers
Outcome efficiency rewards models for being short even when they are wrong
It separates tokens that led to the first correct answer from tokens spent after it, so a long but necessary trace is not penalized
It is the metric the models were trained on
explain: A 3,000-token AIME solution that is correct only at the end has efficiency near 1. A 900-token answer to 2 + 3 that was right after 39 tokens scores 4.3%. Raw length cannot tell these apart.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
question: Ana's laptop runs signature antivirus only. Word starts PowerShell, which downloads nothing to disk and connects to a remote server. Why might the antivirus stay silent?
options: It judges files one at a time, and no file here matches a known-bad signature; the suspicious part is the sequence of behaviours
Antivirus cannot run on laptops that have Office installed
PowerShell disables antivirus whenever it starts
Antivirus only scans email, never processes
explain: Signature antivirus answers a per-file question. Each file here (winword.exe, powershell.exe) is legitimate. The signal is in the relationships: an Office app starting a shell that then goes online. Recording and correlating those relationships is what EDR adds.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Sysmon configuration: include, exclude and rule groups
question: An admin writes `<ProcessAccess onmatch="include" />` with no rules inside, expecting to see every process access. What does Sysmon log for event 10?
options: Every process access
Only access to lsass.exe
Nothing
Only accesses by unsigned programs
explain: An include filter logs only events that match a rule; with no rules nothing matches, so nothing is logged. To log everything you would use an empty exclude filter (which is usually far too noisy for event 10).

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
question: A path rule allows `C:\Windows\*`. Why is that weaker than a publisher rule for Microsoft-signed binaries?
options: Path rules are slower to evaluate
Publisher rules also block Microsoft Office
Some folders under `C:\Windows` are writable by ordinary users, so anything a user copies there is allowed; a publisher rule requires the file's signature instead
Path rules only work for DLLs
explain: A path rule trusts a location. Microsoft's default-rules page names `C:\Windows\Temp` as user-writable, so a path rule over the Windows folder lets users run their own files from there. A publisher rule trusts a signature the user cannot forge.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What EDR can and cannot see
question: Which of these would an endpoint sensor on employees' laptops record?
options: A forwarding rule created in cloud webmail from the attacker's own browser
A login to the company VPN appliance
powershell.exe on a laptop opening a handle to lsass.exe
The content of a TLS connection to a web server
explain: Process-to-process handle requests on a monitored host are exactly what sensors record. The webmail rule and VPN login happen on systems with no sensor, and TLS content is encrypted; only metadata such as the destination is visible.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
question: A 1500 W kettle and a 1500 W space heater (both nearly resistive) live in the same house. Which feature from Hart's pipeline separates them best?
options: Nothing in a single (dP, dQ) step; you need other cues such as typical duration or time of day
Their reactive power steps, since dQ differs
Voltage normalisation, since it rescales each appliance differently
The steady-state tolerance of 35 W
explain: Both are resistive, so dQ is near zero for both and dP matches: the two points land in one cluster. Reactive power only helps when the loads differ in it. Normalisation is applied to the aggregate, not per appliance. Separating them needs extra features such as on-duration or usage patterns, which is why later models add temporal structure.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
question: A team stores only the canonical company ID and discards the raw string to save space. What goes wrong first?
options: Nothing: the canonical ID carries all the information that was in the raw string
Filters become slower because IDs are longer than names
When the matcher makes a mistake or the taxonomy changes, there is no way to audit or re-run normalization on the original input
Fuzzy matching stops working because IDs cannot be compared with edit distance
explain: Normalization is a lossy, model-driven step that will be wrong sometimes and will be improved over time. Keeping the raw string lets you show members what they typed, debug bad merges and re-normalize everything when the alias table or model changes.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
question: Your entity graph has a cluster of 40,000 company records that should be about 30 companies. What is the most likely cause?
options: Blocking was too strict
A few false links between large clusters, chained by transitive connected components
The prior lambda was set too low
explain: Strict blocking and a low prior both cause missed links, which make clusters too small. Giant clusters come from false edges: connected components chains them, so one bad edge between two big clusters merges both.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
question: Which audit activity best catches someone quietly taking over an existing powerful app in your tenant?
options: Update application - Certificates and secrets management (or Add service principal credentials)
Add user
Consent to application
Register device
explain: Taking over an existing app means adding a credential to it, which logs as a certificates and secrets update on the application or added service principal credentials. Consent and new users are other steps of other patterns.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
question: A tenant blocks device code flow everywhere except for the SharePoint resource. A user's session began with a device code sign-in to SharePoint. They then try to open Exchange Online in the same session. What does Microsoft document?
options: Exchange is blocked, because the session is protocol tracked and the device code policy applies to later requests from it
Exchange is allowed because the user signed in normally
Exchange prompts for a new device code
The policy is ignored for refresh tokens
explain: Microsoft's example is exactly this: protocol tracking keeps the session marked as device code through later refreshes, so a sign-in to Exchange in that session is blocked by the authentication flows policy.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
question: Why does Microsoft recommend rolling the AZUREADSSOACC Kerberos decryption key at least every 30 days?
options: Because anyone holding a copy of that key can create tickets Entra ID trusts for synced users, so a regular rollover limits how long a stolen copy stays useful
Because Kerberos tickets expire after 30 days
To change the encryption from AES to RC4
Because the key is needed to sync passwords
explain: Entra ID decrypts Seamless SSO tickets with that key, so a stolen copy works like a silver ticket key for the cloud sign-in. Rolling it regularly, and after any AD compromise, retires old copies.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: Why do event loops set O_NONBLOCK on every socket even though they only read sockets the kernel reported as ready?
options: Because epoll refuses to watch blocking sockets
Because nonblocking reads are faster to copy
Because readiness can be spurious, and one blocking read would stall every other client on the loop
Because blocking sockets cannot be written to
explain: epoll watches blocking sockets just fine. But a readiness report is only a hint: the data may have been discarded, or another thread may have consumed it. With a blocking socket that read would put the only loop thread to sleep, and every other connection would wait with it.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: The only active timer is due in 250 ms, no idle handles are active and nothing is closing. What timeout does libuv pass to the poll step?
options: 0, so it can check the timer often
-1 (infinite), since timers are handled separately
250 ms: sleep until the nearest timer is due unless I/O arrives first
10 ms, a fixed tick
explain: The libuv rules give 0 only when the loop is stopping, has nothing active, has idle handles, or is closing handles. Otherwise the timeout is the time until the closest timer, and infinity only when there are no timers. The I/O wait and the timer wait are one blocking call.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
question: Why did the 17 null variants in the concrete run look better than the baseline on average?
options: The paired t-test is biased toward the variant
Every comparison reused the same baseline run, which happened to score low on these queries, so the tests are correlated
Holm correction shifts p-values downward
The variants were trained on the test queries
explain: The baseline scored 0.357 while its true quality is 0.402. Every variant was compared to that one unlucky draw, so they all looked better together. Shared baselines make multiple tests correlated, which is why the observed FWER (0.421) differs from the independence formula (0.642).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why attackers then reuse existing code
question: Why did NX alone not end memory-corruption exploits?
options: Because NX can be turned off by any program
Because NX only applies to 32-bit processes
Because NX leaks the canary
Because attackers could still redirect control to code that is already executable, such as functions and instruction sequences in libc
explain: NX blocks running data as code, but a hijacked return or function pointer can target existing executable code. That is the core insight of return-into-libc and of Shacham's return-oriented programming paper.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Protecting returns: shadow stacks and pointer authentication
question: An overflow writes past a buffer using an index, skipping the canary and changing only the saved return address. Which mitigation still catches it at return?
options: A hardware shadow stack, because it compares the return address itself with a protected copy
The stack canary
FORTIFY_SOURCE
Partial RELRO
explain: The canary is untouched, so its check passes. The shadow stack compares the actual return address with a copy that normal stores cannot change, so any modification is caught.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Turning mitigations on and checking a binary
question: `readelf -lW prog` shows a GNU_RELRO segment, and `readelf -d prog` shows `FLAGS_1 PIE` but no BIND_NOW or NOW flag. What should you conclude?
options: Partial RELRO and PIE: .got.plt is still writable; add -Wl,-z,now
Full RELRO and PIE
No RELRO, because BIND_NOW is missing
Not PIE, because BIND_NOW is missing
explain: GNU_RELRO alone is partial RELRO. Full RELRO also needs immediate binding (BIND_NOW / NOW). PIE is indicated separately by the PIE flag and the DYN file type.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
question: Under the model with h = 1, C = 100 and b = 50, what is the slowdown S for 8 threads sharing one line?
explain: S = k(1 + C/(b h)) = 8 x (1 + 100/50) = 8 x 3 = 24. The 808 answer is the b = 1 worst case, and 3 forgets to multiply by k: all k threads' writes go through one line, one at a time.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
question: Client A (54 examples) returns 0.10, client B (36) returns 0.80, client C (18) returns 2.70, but this round client B drops out and never reports. What does FedAvg set as the new global model?
options: 0.767, since the weights 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108 are properties of the clients
0.500, the weighted average with client B's contribution set to zero
0.750, the weighted average of A and C renormalized over 72 examples
The round is discarded, because FedAvg requires every selected client
explain: The denominator is m_t, the examples in this round only: 54 + 18 = 72. So the model is (54/72) x 0.10 + (18/72) x 2.70 = 0.075 + 0.675 = 0.750. Keeping stale weights that sum to less than one (option B) would shrink the model toward zero, and single dropouts never abandon a round.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
question: Your DP federated run has far worse accuracy than the non-private baseline at the same epsilon. Which change most directly fixes it, according to the published results?
options: Sample many more users per round, so the same noise is averaged over more clipped updates
Lower the clipping norm S, so each update contributes less
Reduce the number of rounds, since every round spends privacy budget
Switch from user-level to example-level accounting and report that instead
explain: Noise is added once per round to the average, so more users per round shrinks its relative size at fixed epsilon: matching the baseline needed about 5000 users per round instead of 100, roughly 60x the compute. Lowering S adds clipping bias, and with large populations extra rounds cost very little budget (epsilon moved from 0.84 to 0.88 over a million rounds at 1e9 users).

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
question: An MoE layer has 16 experts, each the same size as the dense MLP it replaced, with top-2 routing. Compared with the dense MLP, what happens to parameters and per-token FLOPs in that layer?
options: Both grow 16 times
Parameters grow 2 times; FLOPs grow 16 times
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs grow about 2 times, plus a tiny router cost
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs stay exactly the same as dense
explain: Every expert is stored, so parameters scale with N = 16. Each token runs only K = 2 experts, so expert FLOPs are 2 times the dense MLP. The router (one dot product per expert) adds a little on top. With top-1 routing (Switch), expert FLOPs would match the dense MLP.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
question: A team copies V3's recipe but trains with very small global batches (a few sequences per step). Which risk grows most?
options: Future-token leakage from the bias
The shared expert stops training
Node-limited routing stops working
Per-step load imbalance, since batch-wise balancing cannot even out a batch that is mostly one domain, so busy experts stall the step
explain: The loss-free paper shows balance improving as the computation batch grows, and the V3 report lists imbalance within small batches as a challenge that large-scale expert and data parallelism (model copies each training on a different slice of the batch) solves. The bias uses only past batches, so there is no leakage.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 forward: when the exponential is the bottleneck
question: Why does FlashAttention-4 emulate only 10 to 25% of exponentials in software instead of all of them?
options: The polynomial is too inaccurate for more than a quarter of the row
Emulation uses extra registers, register bandwidth and latency; doing all of them would cause spills and leave MUFU idle
FMA units can only process one row in four
MUFU is faster than the FMA units for every input
explain: The goal is to split the work between two units that can run in parallel. The paper says full emulation would raise register pressure and could cause spills that cancel the gain, so the fraction is tuned to the MMA-to-exp ratio of each tile shape. Accuracy is not the limit: after BF16 rounding the polynomial matches hardware.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Attention states, cascade attention and composable formats
question: Partial states for one query: prefix $(O = 2.0, \mathrm{LSE} = 0)$ and suffix $(O = 6.0, \mathrm{LSE} = 0)$. What is the merged output?
options: 6.0, the larger LSE wins
It cannot be computed without the raw scores
explain: Equal LSEs mean both halves carry equal total softmax mass, so the weights are $e^0/(e^0+e^0) = 0.5$ each and $O = 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0.5 \cdot 6 = 4.0$. The merged LSE is $\log 2$. The states alone are enough; that is the whole point of the operator.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
question: Which statement about conditional flow matching is correct?
options: It needs the marginal velocity field computed over the whole dataset at every step
It only works with straight-line paths
Regressing onto per-sample conditional velocities gives the same gradient as regressing onto the intractable marginal velocity
It trains by maximizing the log-likelihood of the data under the ODE
explain: Lipman et al. Theorem 2: the CFM and FM losses differ by a constant independent of the parameters, so their gradients match. Straight OT paths are one choice; diffusion-style Gaussian paths also fit the framework.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
question: A race fires in 1 of every 184,756 equally likely orders. Your CI runs the test 1,000 times a day, each run picking an order at random. Which statement is closest to right?
options: Over a week you have roughly a 4% chance of having seen the bug even once
After a week of green runs the code is very likely correct
The bug is impossible in practice because its probability is so small
Running the test on more cores makes the bug certain to appear
explain: 7,000 runs give $1-(1-1/184756)^{7000} \approx 3.7\%$. Green CI says little here. Rare orders still happen in production, where the same code runs billions of times; AWS noted that improbability is not a defense against such bugs.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Modeling a distributed protocol: messages, loss and duplication
question: Why does TwoPhase.tla need no Lose action to check safety?
options: TLC assumes a reliable network unless told otherwise
Message loss cannot break safety in any protocol
Sets automatically drop messages at random
No action is ever forced to receive a message, so a lost message looks the same as one that is never received
explain: Safety specs only allow steps, they never require them. A behavior in which nobody reads a message is already included, and that is exactly what loss looks like. Loss matters for liveness, where fairness would otherwise force the receive.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, VerusSync and what a proof trusts
question: Your team is designing a new lease-based leader handoff for a replicated store and has two weeks. Where should formal effort go first?
options: A TLA+ spec of the handoff protocol with crashes and message loss, model checked with 3 nodes
Verus proofs of every Rust function in the storage engine
TLAPS proofs of liveness
Nothing formal; add more integration tests
explain: Design bugs in protocols are the cheapest to find with a model checker, and a wrong design makes correct code pointless. AWS's experience: specs of a few hundred lines found bugs in weeks. Code proofs cost several proof lines per code line, and TLAPS liveness proofs need hand-written fairness and temporal reasoning, far more effort than a model check.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
question: Two data-parallel ranks quantize their gradients to FP8 with their own per-tensor scales and run a standard all-reduce on the raw FP8 values. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because all-reduce is a sum and sums commute
The all-reduce overflows on every step
NCCL rejects FP8 tensors
The summed values mix two different scales, so no single scale decodes the sum correctly
explain: Each stored value means value divided by its own rank's scale. Adding 3 (scale 1000) and 12 (scale 4000) gives 15, which decodes to neither 0.006 nor anything meaningful. FP8-LM all-reduces the minimum scale first, requantizes, and only then sums.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4
question: In part 5 the output error stayed near 13.5% from K = 256 to K = 4096. Which change would make output error grow with K?
options: Using a larger random seed
Replacing round-to-nearest with stochastic rounding on both inputs
Using 32-value blocks instead of 16
Summing the products in a 14-bit float instead of float64, so each add onto a growing sum loses its low bits
explain: Input rounding errors scale with the signal. Random-sign errors grow like sqrt(K), as the signal of random data does; a one-way bias grows like K, but so does the signal of same-sign data, so the ratio stays flat. What grows with K is the accumulator: lesson 3's 14-bit running sum adds each product onto an ever coarser grid, which is why DeepSeek promotes partial sums to FP32.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Group commit: one WAL flush makes many transactions durable
question: A WAL device needs 4 ms per flush and is busy flushing all the time. On average each flush carries 10 commit records. What is the commit throughput?
options: 250 commits/s
2,500 commits/s
40 commits/s
25,000 commits/s
explain: X = B / F = 10 / 0.004 s = 2,500 commits/s. Without sharing (B = 1) the same device tops out at 250/s.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Fuzzing from a stormy night in 1988: random, mutation, generation
question: What did Miller's original fuzz study use as its oracle?
options: A specification of each utility's correct output
Code coverage reached by each input
A comparison with a second implementation
Whether the program crashed or hung
explain: The oracle was deliberately simple: crash or hang means fail. That is why it could be automated across many programs and operating systems with no model of what each program should do.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Sanitizers as oracles: which bug each one catches
question: The TSan run printed hits = 200000, the correct total. Why is the report still a real bug?
options: It is not; the output proves the code is correct
TSan always reports false positives on counters
The total is only correct because of TSan
A race is undefined behaviour; this run got lucky, other compilers, optimisation levels or timings can lose updates
explain: TSan reports the unsynchronised access itself, not a wrong answer. Correct output on one run proves nothing about the next one, which is exactly why a race detector beats checking results.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed
question: How was Cloudbleed actually discovered?
options: A fuzzer crashed Cloudflare's edge servers
Cloudflare's monitoring alerted on high memory use
A customer reported a wrong page
Data gathered for fuzzing corpora contained leaked memory that did not match what Tavis Ormandy expected
explain: Ormandy's Project Zero report describes a corpus distillation project: public data collected to build fuzzing corpora contained uninitialised memory. Fuzzing infrastructure found it, but not by crashing anything.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Variant analysis and patch diffing: one bug, many siblings
question: Why did fuzzing find new Bash bugs after the first Shellshock patch?
options: The patch introduced them
AFL is better than code review at all bugs
The bugs were in a different program
The first patch only blocked one symptom; the function-import parser, still reachable from untrusted environment variables, had more bugs that AFL's coverage feedback explored
explain: Zalewski's write-up: AFL derived about 1,000 distinct test cases from one seed function definition and found CVE-2014-6277 and 6278 in the same parser. The robust fix stopped untrusted variables from reaching it.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
question: You only accept matches with at most 1 edit. The query has 6 characters and a candidate has 9. How much of the DP table must you fill to reject the candidate?
options: All 7 x 10 cells
Only the diagonal band of width 3
None: the length difference already proves the distance is at least 3
Only the last row
explain: Every character of length difference needs at least one insertion or deletion, so $d \ge 9-6 = 3 > 1$. A length check is the cheapest filter of all and real implementations apply it before touching the table.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
question: SymSpell with k = 1 finds that the query and a dictionary word share a one-character delete, while neither is a delete of the other. What kind of single error explains that?
options: An insertion in the query
A deletion in the query
A substitution or an adjacent transposition
Nothing; it is a false positive that cannot be within 1 edit
explain: A shared one-character delete fits one differing position (a substitution, like reieve from recieve and relieve) or an adjacent swap (receve from recieve and receive). It does not guarantee 1 edit: abc and bca share the delete bc but are 2 edits apart, so SymSpell verifies every candidate with a real distance.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Searching code space: kd-trees, tolerance and why quads beat triangles
question: Why did quint (5-star) indexes solve images more slowly than quads, even though a quint match is almost always correct?
options: 6D kd-tree lookups are impossible
The solver must try many quints before finding one whose 5 stars are all in both the image and the index, and higher-dimensional search is slower
Quint codes are not scale invariant
Quints produce more coincidental matches than triangles
explain: The paper reports that for over 80% of solved images the first quint match found was correct. The cost is elsewhere: the chance that all 5 stars are detected and catalogued is lower, so many more quints are tried, and near-neighbor search slows with dimension.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
question: Which statement about two geohashes is always true?
options: If both points share a 6-character prefix at the equator, they are at most about 1.35 km apart
If two points are less than 100 m apart, they share at least a 5-character prefix
Geohashes that are adjacent in sort order are always in adjacent cells
Two points with no shared prefix are at least 1,000 km apart
explain: A shared 6-character prefix means both points are in one cell of 1.2 km x 609.4 m, whose diagonal is about 1.35 km. The other statements fail at cell boundaries: the London pair is 69 m apart with no shared prefix, and the Z-order curve jumps between quadrants.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Pixels in memory: NHWC, NCHW, pitch and a warp's 96 bytes
question: A color-convert kernel reads an RGB8 (uchar3) NHWC image with one pixel per thread. Why is the per-instruction load efficiency about 33 percent?
options: The image rows are not padded, so the second row starts unaligned
Each channel load has stride 3 across lanes, so its sectors carry three times the bytes that one instruction uses
NHWC always loses to NCHW because planes are contiguous
A warp of 32 threads cannot cover 96 bytes in fewer than 32 transactions
explain: A uchar3 has alignment 1, so a pixel is three separate 1-byte accesses. Each of those instructions touches 32 addresses that are 3 bytes apart, spanning 96 bytes of sectors to deliver 32 useful bytes. The warp's total footprint is still contiguous, which is why the fix is a wider access (a 4-pixel carrier or an RGBA8 format), not a different layout.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo
question: A 16x16 block computing one output per thread stages a tile for a 9x9 filter. How large is the tile, and how much of it is halo?
options: 16x16 = 256 elements, no halo, because shared memory is indexed per thread
25x25 = 625 elements, of which 369 are halo
24x24 = 576 elements, of which 320 are halo: 2.25 loads per output
32x32 = 1024 elements, rounded up to the warp size
explain: The tile is (16 + 9 - 1) square = 24x24 = 576 elements for 256 outputs, so 320 halo elements and 2.25 loads per output. The halo is k - 1 = 8 elements across both dimensions together, not k, because a radius-4 window needs 4 extra on each side.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
question: Tensor A is allocated on s0, read by a kernel on s1, then deleted without record_stream. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; the allocator always waits for all streams before reuse
The allocator raises an error because A was used on two streams
The block leaks and is never reused
s0 can reuse A's block for a new tensor while s1's kernel is still reading it
explain: Without record_stream the allocator only knows about s0. Reuse on s0 is ordered after s0's work, but nothing orders it after s1's kernel, so the new tensor can overwrite data s1 is still using.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
question: A row-major `float` matrix has `ld = 4096` columns. A kernel with 32 x 32 blocks computes `int r = blockIdx.y*32 + threadIdx.x; int c = blockIdx.x*32 + threadIdx.y;` and reads `a[r*ld + c]`. How many sectors does each warp load request?
options: 4, because the warp reads 32 floats
8, because the matrix is large
1, because all threads share c
32, because consecutive threads are 4096 floats apart
explain: Within a warp threadIdx.y is fixed and threadIdx.x runs 0 to 31, so it is r that varies. Consecutive threads are ld = 4096 floats (16 KB) apart, each in its own sector: 32 sectors per request and 12.5% efficiency. Swapping which index uses threadIdx.x fixes it.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
question: A colleague reports: "Nsight Systems says the GPU is 97 percent utilized, so the GPU is the bottleneck and we need better kernels." What is the hole in that reasoning?
options: Nothing: 97 percent time utilization means the SMs are 97 percent busy
Utilization there is time based, so a long exposed memcpy or a tiny kernel occupying one SM counts as full utilization
Nsight Systems cannot measure GPU utilization at all, only CPU time
It is wrong only if the application uses more than one CUDA stream
explain: The rule's own notes say the utilization is time utilization, not resource utilization: a single running memcpy counts the same as a huge kernel, and concurrent operations can sum past 100 percent. 97 percent busy could be 97 percent copying, or one kernel with a 1-block grid. Per-kernel counters, not timeline utilization, tell you whether the hardware is actually being used.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
question: Which single profiling decision most often invalidates a comparison between two versions of a kernel?
options: Changing the capture configuration between the two runs, for example clock, cache or replay settings
Profiling on a GPU that has a display attached
Using the basic section set instead of the full one
Reporting durations in microseconds rather than milliseconds
explain: Both the triage guide and the profiling guide insist on it: keep capture settings stable while comparing runs, and keep cache-control and replay settings identical unless the policy itself is the variable under test. A display-attached GPU adds noise and a smaller section set loses detail, but a changed control turns a measurement into an incomparable one.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
question: Which barrier placement is valid?
options: `if (blockIdx.x % 2 == 0) { __syncthreads(); }`
`if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0) { __syncthreads(); }`
`if (threadIdx.x < 64) { __syncthreads(); }`
`for (int k = 0; k < threadIdx.x; ++k) __syncthreads();`
explain: blockIdx.x is the same for every thread in a block, so the condition is uniform across the block and either all of its threads reach the barrier or none do. The other three depend on threadIdx, so some threads of the block skip or repeat the barrier: undefined behavior.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
question: Community X has internal weight $L_X = 4$ and degree sum $k_X = 12$ in a graph with $m = 20$. What is its modularity term?
explain: $L_X/m = 4/20 = 0.20$ and $(k_X/2m)^2 = (12/40)^2 = 0.09$, so the term is 0.11. Dividing by $m$ rather than $2m$ in the second term is the common slip.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
question: FastGraphRAG builds relationships from co-occurrence instead of LLM extraction. What do you lose?
options: Community detection, which then cannot run
Relationship and entity descriptions; edges only say that two noun phrases appeared in the same text unit, so the graph is noisier
The ability to answer global questions at all
All embeddings
explain: The docs say FastGraphRAG has no entity or relationship descriptions and a noisier graph. Leiden and community reports still run, which is why it remains useful for global summary questions.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: The GRPO objective token by token: clipping, averaging and KL
question: Why does GRPO put the KL penalty in the loss rather than subtracting it from the reward like PPO for RLHF?
options: The KL in the loss is cheaper to compute
Folding a per-token KL into the reward would mix it into the group-normalized advantage, which is meant to be a pure comparison of sibling rewards
The reward cannot be negative
PPO's KL estimator is biased
explain: DeepSeekMath says adding the KL to the loss avoids complicating the advantage calculation. GRPO has no critic to spread a per-token reward over the sequence; its advantage is one standardized outcome per output.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: GTFS Realtime messages and decoding them in Python
question: A consumer receives FULL_DATASET feeds every 30 s. At 08:10 the feed has a TripUpdate for T1. At 08:10:30 it does not. What should the app show for T1?
options: No realtime information: fall back to the schedule and say so, or hide the prediction
Keep the 08:10 prediction until a new one arrives
Mark T1 as canceled
Assume T1 is now exactly on time
explain: Each FULL_DATASET message is the whole state. A dropped entity means there is no realtime information for it now. It is not a cancellation (that is an explicit CANCELED), and the reference warns that absence must not be read as on time.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
question: After a change, a service's IPC rises from 0.8 to 1.6, but requests take exactly as long as before. What is the most plausible explanation?
options: The counters are broken, since higher IPC always means faster code
The CPU clock frequency doubled
IPC is measured per core, so it cannot change per request
Cycles per request stayed the same while instructions per request doubled, for example from spinning or extra work
explain: IPC is a ratio. If time and cycles are unchanged, doubling IPC means twice as many instructions were retired per request: busy-waiting or redundant work. That is why IPC must be read alongside the raw instruction count.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
question: On a cloud VM, `perf stat` prints `<not supported>` for cycles and instructions but shows task-clock and page-faults. Why?
options: The hypervisor does not expose the hardware PMU to this guest, so only software events work
perf is too old to know these events
The program ran too briefly to count any cycles
Those events need the :u modifier
explain: task-clock and page-faults are software events maintained by the kernel. Hardware events need PMU access, which a guest only gets if the hypervisor virtualizes it.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Branchless selection and secret-independent memory access
question: You compile the mask-based ct_select and find a conditional branch in the assembly. What is the right conclusion?
options: The source is wrong; masks always compile to branches
The compiler is free to do this because C does not promise timing; use a vetted primitive or a compiler barrier and re-check
Branches are fine as long as the branch predictor is accurate
Switch to -O0, which guarantees constant time
explain: C's semantics cover results, not timing, so optimisers may reintroduce branches. Libraries use techniques such as value barriers, and you verify the output. -O0 gives no such guarantee either.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Meltdown: reading kernel memory, and why KPTI fixes it
question: Which workload should you expect to slow down most after enabling KPTI on an older CPU without PCID?
options: A numerical simulation that rarely calls the kernel
A small-message server doing many system calls per request
A GPU training job
A program that only reads from its own heap
explain: The cost is paid on every kernel entry and exit (CR3 switches and TLB flushes without PCID). System-call-heavy code pays most, as the roughly 50 percent microbenchmark slowdown shows.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Trusted hardware: TPMs, measured boot and secure enclaves
question: BitLocker seals the disk key to PCR values. An attacker replaces the bootloader with one that logs keystrokes. What happens at the next boot?
options: The TPM detects the new bootloader's signature and deletes the key
Nothing: PCRs only record the kernel
The bootloader's hash changes the PCR value, so the TPM refuses to unseal the key and recovery is needed
The attacker's bootloader can reset the PCR to the old value
explain: Extend is one-way and order-sensitive, and the first 16 PCRs reset only with the TPM. A different bootloader produces different PCRs, so the sealed key stays locked.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
question: A pool has 10 free pages and no reservations. Process A maps 8 huge pages with MAP_HUGETLB and touches 2 of them. Process B then tries to mmap 4 huge pages with MAP_HUGETLB. What happens?
options: B's mmap succeeds because HugePages_Free is 8
B's mmap succeeds, but B gets SIGBUS when it touches its third page
B's mmap fails with ENOMEM: Free is 8 but 6 are reserved for A, leaving 2
The kernel reclaims A's untouched reserved pages and gives them to B
explain: After A: Free = 10 - 2 = 8 and Rsvd = 8 - 2 = 6. Only Free - Rsvd = 2 pages are available, so B's 4-page reservation fails at mmap time. Reservations are not stolen back, and failing in mmap rather than at fault time is the whole point of reserving.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
question: Which task is least likely to separate a pure SSM from a Transformer of the same size and data?
options: Recalling a phone number listed 3,000 tokens earlier
Copying a long string from the prompt
Zero-shot commonsense multiple choice such as PIQA or HellaSwag
Few-shot classification that must reuse exact label strings
explain: PIQA asks which of two solutions achieves an everyday physical goal; HellaSwag asks for the most plausible ending of a described situation. On such zero-shot commonsense tasks Mamba and Mamba-2 matched or beat the Transformer in the NVIDIA 8B study. The other three all need exact retrieval or copying from the context, which is where fixed-state models fall behind.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Serving a hybrid: prefix caching, rollback and chunked prefill
question: A server snapshots SSM states only at branch points found by Marconi-style speculative insertion, plus after each request's last decoded token. A new system prompt appears in requests 1, 2 and 3, each with a different question. Which is the first request whose Mamba layers can reuse the prompt?
options: Request 1
Request 2
Request 3
None of them, since recurrent states cannot be shared
explain: Request 1 creates the tree entry; nothing is shared yet. Request 2's insertion splits that edge at the end of the shared prompt, so its prefill saves the states there. Request 3 is the first to hit them. The paper accepts missing the second occurrence because hot prefixes are shared by many requests.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
question: You convert a 32-layer Transformer with 128 KiB of KV per token into a hybrid that keeps 1 attention layer in 8. How much KV per token remains?
options: 16 KiB
32 KiB
4 KiB
64 KiB
explain: KV is per attention layer: 128 KiB / 32 layers = 4 KiB per layer, and 4 layers remain, so 16 KiB, an 8x saving at long context. The Mamba layers add a fixed state that does not grow with context.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Why a raw query is a poor probe for an unsupervised encoder
question: A team has a new internal wiki, no click logs and no labeled queries. Which statement about their options is accurate?
options: A supervised dense retriever cannot be trained on in-domain labels yet, which is exactly the setting HyDE targets
They must label at least MS MARCO scale data before any dense retrieval works
BM25 is guaranteed to beat every dense method here
Contriever alone will match a fine-tuned retriever
explain: No relevance labels is the zero-shot setting of the HyDE paper. Contriever alone is usable but weak; BM25 is a strong baseline but not guaranteed best. The paper's answer is to move relevance modeling into a generative LLM.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
question: Your stack already uses a strong cross-encoder reranker that scores 72 nDCG@10 on your eval. A teammate wants to add generated passages to the reranker's query. Based on Weller et al., what should you expect and do?
options: A guaranteed gain, as on DPR
Likely no gain or a loss; measure on your own eval before shipping, and consider expansions only for the first stage or for shifted domains
No effect either way
A gain only if N is at least 8
explain: Weller et al. found strong models are generally harmed: MonoT5-3B lost 4.0 on DL19 and 14.7 on FiQA. Expansion tends to help weaker models or large format shifts, so it must be evaluated, not assumed.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: The Purdue model: levels from field devices to the enterprise
question: Why does NIST say outbound rules from the control network should be as strict as inbound ones?
options: Because outbound traffic is always faster
Because PLCs send too many emails
Because an infected control-network machine that can reach the internet or enterprise freely gives attackers a channel out and a path back in
Because inbound rules do not work in OT
explain: Malware on a Level 2 or 3 host needs to talk to its operator. Strict egress filtering blocks that and limits what a compromised host can reach. NIST calls unmanaged outbound connections 'a significant risk'.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied
question: An engineer uploads the PLC program through the plant's engineering workstation and it matches the approved version exactly. Why might that not be enough after a Stuxnet-style infection?
options: The workstation's PLC communication library may be intercepted, so the tool shows a cleaned view while the PLC runs extra code
Uploads are always encrypted
PLCs cannot store more than one program
Hashes cannot be computed for PLC code
explain: Stuxnet's fake s7otbxdx.dll hid its blocks from Step 7 reads. Verification must use a trusted path: a clean machine, vendor integrity features, or physical inspection of behaviour.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
question: A plant wants dashboards in the head office showing live tank levels, and wants no possible inbound path. Which design fits?
options: A unidirectional gateway pushing historian data to a replica in the DMZ, read by the head office
A firewall rule allowing the head office to query the PLCs
A VPN from head office into the control zone
Putting the PLCs on the internet behind a password
explain: A data diode is physically one-way, so the replica can be fed without any route back into OT. Firewalls and VPNs can be misconfigured to allow inbound traffic; a diode cannot.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
question: In federation, what does the service provider actually verify when Ana arrives?
options: Ana's password, forwarded by the IdP
That Ana's browser has an IdP cookie
A signed statement from the IdP, checked with the IdP's public key it stored in advance
Ana's MFA code, relayed by the browser
explain: NIST's definition: the RP does not verify the subscriber's authenticators. It verifies the IdP's signed assertion with a key from the trust agreement, and the IdP's own cookie belongs to the IdP's domain, which the app cannot read.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Validating a SAML response: every check, and the replay cache
question: The SP runs on three servers behind a load balancer, each with its own in-memory replay cache. What is the weakness?
options: None
The caches will overflow
An attacker can replay a captured assertion to a server that has not seen it yet
The IdP cannot sign for three servers
explain: A replay cache only works if every server that can accept the assertion consults it. Use a shared store with entries that expire at the assertion's NotOnOrAfter.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
question: During a planned rollover, why does the IdP publish the new key in metadata days before signing with it?
options: To give attackers less time
Because certificates take days to issue
So every SP has refreshed its metadata and trusts the new key before the first assertion signed with it arrives
To keep the metadata file small
explain: SPs refresh metadata on their own schedules. Publishing first and switching later means no SP ever receives an assertion signed with a key it does not know, so logins do not break.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: IdP compromise and Golden SAML: forging the whole federation
question: In the 2023 attacks Okta described, how did attackers impersonate users without stealing a signing key?
options: By cracking password hashes
By wrapping XML signatures
By using Super Administrator access to add a second IdP they controlled, whose assertions the org trusted
By replaying old assertions
explain: Okta reported a second IdP configured as an "impersonation app" through inbound federation, with usernames manipulated to match real users. Changing the trust configuration is as powerful as stealing a key, which is why IdP creation events deserve alerts.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
question: In the script, Ben's db:admin grant was approved by Ben. Why is that a finding even though a request exists?
options: Because database access should never be requested
Because a request without a ticket number is invalid
Because the person who benefits approved it, so no second person ever judged the need
Because admin rights can only be granted by HR
explain: An approval is a second person's judgment. When the requester approves their own request, the record looks complete but no independent check happened. This is the core of separation of duties (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Role mining and role engineering: from a pile of grants to roles
question: A mined role for the support team includes the permission to delete customer accounts, because most support staff happen to hold it today. What should happen before the role is adopted?
options: Adopt it: mining reflects what people use
Remove the support team from RBAC entirely
The role owner checks each permission against the job; holding something widely is not evidence it is needed
Split the role so each person has a personal role
explain: Mining reproduces current access, including widespread over-provisioning. An owner must validate the role. Personal roles would recreate the original mess.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Bastions, jump hosts and session brokering
